newsitem.title: BRAZIL: SOYBEANS--Brazil govt gets going on first estimate.
newsitem.headline: SOYBEANS--Brazil govt gets going on first estimate.

text.p: Agronomists from the National Supply Company (Conab) of Brazil's Agriculture Ministry are to leave for the field next week to conduct the first surveys of soybean planting prospects, a Conab technician said.
"Our people will be travelling on October 13 and should return by October 19 so we would hope to have a first estimate by the following week," said Airton Camargo Pacheco.
Provisional forecasts for the 1996/97 soybean crop, including that of the U.S. Department of Agriculture released today, continue to be around 26 million tonnes.
But much will depend on the release of farmer credit and availability of seeds, Pacheco said.
"Producers are currently pressing the government to release money in time but there is already talk of a seed shortage. I think it will not be easy to manage 26 million tonnes," he said.
So far there does not seem to be any obvious reasons why the two top-producing states of Rio Grande do Sul and Parana should not see good production of around six million tonnes each.
Last year a prolonged drought in Rio Grande do Sul saw output drop to 4.4 million tonnes from 5.85 million in 1994, with the state pushed into second place in the production stakes behind Parana.

But earlier this week a representative from the state co-operatives' federation said output this year should hopefully exceed six million tonnes and that Rio Grande do Sul should resume its traditional place at the top of the league.
This view was shared by Conab's Pacheco.
"I think that if they repeat the same planted area as before, they could return to first place," he said.
Parana is also optimistic, with initial projections by the state agricultural secretariat of production at 6.2 million to 7.5 million tonnes against 6.38 million tonnes last year.

Other states which are hoping to show substantive increases are Santa Catarina, where producers are talking of a possible eight percent increase in planted area of 222,000 hectares last year, and Goias, where expectations are of an 11 percent rise.
Last year Goias saw a fall in planted area to 900,000 hectares from 1.1 million the previous year, with output slipping to two million tonnes from 2.1 million in 1994/95.
"The fall was around eight percent so if we see an 11 percent increase this year, it means there will be a slight rise overall," Pacheco said.
The two much smaller producing states of Maranhao and Piaui also have good potential to increase output, he added.
In Maranhao, where planted area of 90,000 hectares yielded 200,000 tonnes last year, expectations are of an additional 30,000 hectares.
In Piaui, where output was 23,000 tonnes in 1995/96, farmers may be able this year to use land which has been paralysed for financial reasons to improve on last year's 12,000 hectares.

On the negative side, farmers in the third largest producing state of Mato Grosso have already warned debt problems will lead possibly to a 15 percent drop in planted area and crop size after output of 4.4 million tonnes in 1995.
While acknowledging the severity of farmers' debt problems in the state, the gloomy forecasts could contain an element of sabre-rattling, Conab's Pacheco said.
"I think they are basically trying to frighten the government into action," he said.
-- Rio de Janeiro newsroom, 5521 5074151
